title: Phoebe of Cenchreae
aliases: tell me about phoebe of cenchreae
why is phoebe of cenchreae important
summary: A minister or deacon associated with the assembly at Cenchreae whom Paul commends to the Roman assemblies as a prostatis of many, including himself.
historical_context: Romans 16:1-2 is the only secure primary notice. Cenchreae was Corinth's eastern port, making travel toward the Aegean and Rome plausible, but the text does not explicitly call Phoebe the letter carrier, identify her household, or specify a formal office.
ancient_near_east_context: Phoebe belongs to a Greco-Roman port and diaspora-Jewish-Christian network rather than a generic Ancient Near Eastern setting.
second_temple_context: The commendation belongs to a first-century Jewish and gentile Christ-following network in Roman Corinthia and Rome, before a complete separation of Judaism and Christianity.
canonical_context: Romans names Phoebe before the greetings of chapter 16. Diakonos and prostatis ground debates about ministry, patronage, leadership, and letter delivery, but later titles must not be read back without argument.
literary_context: Acts and the Epistles use Phoebe of Cenchreae to display gospel partnership and ecclesial formation.
covenantal_significance: Phoebe of Cenchreae participates in the nations' inclusion and the building up of the body of Christ.
canonical_role: Phoebe of Cenchreae serves as a canonical person anchor, connecting biographical context, key passages, and related places, events, and themes.

related_objects.notes: Romans 16:1-2 is the primary canonical evidence for Phoebe.
Patron, benefactor, leader, and helper readings require lexical and social qualification.
The cluster supplies bounded Cenchreae, travel, household, and patronage context.
The Rome cluster bounds commendation, probable letter travel, reception, hospitality, and title interpretation.
The synthesis distinguishes Phoebe's explicit commendation and titles from probable travel and disputed later-office equivalence.

interpretive_notes.note: These figures are best read as part of the church's shared mission rather than isolated heroes.
